To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
jurors' understanding of the instructions they receive is limited, and that the instructions they receive are vague.

(1) the law of damages in tort and contract is ambiguous; (2) this ambiguity is necessary to achieve the goal of providing individualized justice across a wide range of factual circumstances; (3) the law of torts and contracts is vague and ambiguous, which is necessary to achieve individualized justice; (4) this vagueness and ambiguity makes jury instructions on damages difficult to write; (5) this vaguenesses and ambiguity makes the jury instructions difficult to understand, and

(1) jurors' comprehension and application of instructions related to damages are influenced by the specific language of the instructions, the manner in which they are presented, and by other trial factors; (2) these factors can be manipulated to improve the clarity and consistency of jury instructions on damages; and (3) the vagueness in the instructions is not a result of a failure to instruct the jurors on the law but is a result of the purposeful ambiguity in the substantive law itself.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the jury instructions on damages, the effects of procedural variations at trial on jurors' comprehension and application of instructions, and the effects of instruction reform efforts.
